title: 'Healthy' Snacks May Not Be: What a Nutritionist Says About Millet Chips, Ragi Cookies and Makhana
excerpt: Nutritionist Lakshmi Kale tells Hindustan Times' 'Indian Food Decoded' that processing, oil and salt can undo the benefits of millet, ragi and vegetable ingredients in packaged snacks.
body:
• Millet chips, jowar puffs and ragi snacks may contain nutritious whole grains — but processing with starch, oil, salt and flavourings can undo much of the benefit, says nutritionist Lakshmi Kale.
  • Vegetable chips are the biggest health halo of all: a packet of beetroot chips does not count as a serving of vegetables.
  • A nutritious ingredient can be part of a snack without making the entire snack nutritionally equivalent to the original food, Kale explains.
  • The advice applies across the aisle — protein bars, seed crackers, baked namkeen, roasted makhana and quinoa snacks all deserve the same label scrutiny.

Walk into a supermarket today and the snack aisle looks like a health store. Millet chips, ragi cookies, jowar puffs, protein bars, seed crackers, beetroot chips, spinach chips, baked namkeen, roasted makhana, quinoa snacks — the options are endless. But how healthy are these snacks really? In the latest edition of Hindustan Times' Tezzbuzz Lifestyle series "Indian Food Decoded," nutritionist Lakshmi Kale, head nutritionist at Nutrition In Sync, decoded what is actually inside some of our favourite "healthy" snacks.

The Grain-Chip Illusion

Millets are nutritious whole grains — that much is true. But once they are turned into a highly processed chip and combined with starch, oil, salt and flavourings, the fact that millet is in the recipe does not make the entire packet a healthy food. The same applies to jowar puffs, ragi snacks and multigrain crackers.

The grain used matters, but so does the final product. Processing can significantly change a snack's nutritional profile, and a wholesome-sounding base ingredient can end up as a minor component of a product that is mostly starch, oil and salt.

"A nutritious ingredient can be part of a snack without making the entire snack nutritionally equivalent to the original food."

— Lakshmi Kale, head nutritionist at Nutrition In Sync

Vegetable Chips Don't Count as Vegetables

Then there are vegetable chips, which Kale suggests may be the biggest health halo of all. Beetroot chips, carrot chips, okra chips, spinach chips — they look colourful, sound wholesome and make the eater feel virtuous. But a packet of beetroot chips is still a packaged snack. As Kale puts it, it doesn't count as a vegetable serving simply because beetroot was involved somewhere in the process — and depending on how the chips are made, they can bring along quite a bit of oil and salt.

The vegetable itself isn't the problem. The problem is the assumption that the word "vegetable" on the packet automatically makes the finished product healthy.

The Rest of the Aisle

The same scrutiny applies across the board. Protein bars, seed crackers, baked namkeen, roasted makhana and quinoa snacks have all ridden the wellness wave, and many are genuinely better than the chips they replace. But they vary enormously in quality. Roasted makhana with minimal seasoning is a different product from a heavily flavoured makhana pack; a protein bar built on dates and nuts is different from one built on syrups and fillers. The label, not the category, tells the truth.

How to Actually Read a Label

Kale's framework is simple: look past the hero ingredient and judge the finished product. Check the ingredient list for the order and proportion of starches, oils and flavourings; compare the sodium and saturated fat per serving against whole-food equivalents; and be sceptical of front-of-pack claims that lean on a single virtuous ingredient. Packaged snacks marketed as healthy are increasingly popular, and supermarkets are happy to oblige — but the presence of a nutritious ingredient does not automatically make the finished product healthy.
